Peering into the crystal ball: experts predict the future of RWE, HTA, and value-based healthcare in 2025
19 December 2024

2024 was a year of significant progress in real-world evidence (RWE), health technology assessment (HTA), and value-based care, and it certainly kept The Evidence Base team busy as we covered these important developments. From advancements in regulatory frameworks to innovations in real-world data (RWD) utilization, the past year has been marked by many achievements that have laid the groundwork for the future of healthcare decision-making. As we predicted, the rapid integration of AI, evolving HTA methodologies, and an increasing emphasis on patient-centered outcomes have continued to redefine the landscape.

But what lies ahead for 2025? In this article, we bring together insights from key stakeholders and experts to explore their predictions for the future, highlighting the trends and challenges that will shape the field in the coming year.

Regulatory and policy transformations
For Stuart McCully, author of our ‘What’s in a Name’ series, 2025 is set to be a transformative year for real-world research (RWR), particularly in the EU, with groundbreaking regulatory changes on the horizon. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) is advancing its vision of fully integrating RWE into regulatory processes through initiatives like DARWIN-EU and the European Health Data Space (EHDS), which will provide unprecedented access to pseudonymized patient health data.

Starting January 2025, as McCully explains to The Evidence Base, the EU Health Technology Assessment Regulation (HTAR) will require drug and device manufacturers to plan evidence strategies, including RWE, earlier than ever before. Additionally, the anticipated publication and initial implementation of new EU drug laws will promote RWD use, advanced analytics, and patient involvement.

In his opinion, these developments underscore a shift toward recognizing RWE as indispensable in the drug development lifecycle, heralding a new era of innovation and collaboration.

“Real-world data and evidence are no longer secondary considerations in developing target product profiles and integrated evidence plans. Instead, they are becoming indispensable complements to clinical trial data. These regulatory changes signal a shift toward recognising the value of RWE early in the drug development lifecycle.”

From an international perspective, Rachele Hendricks-Sturrup (Research Director for Real-World Evidence at the Duke-Robert J. Margolis, MD, Institute for Health Policy) sees 2025 as a pivotal moment to tackle the shortcomings of RWE. She anticipates a sharper focus within the community on areas where RWE has underperformed, coupled with increased trust and transparency between industry and regulators. She highlights the opportunity to identify where RWE has proven effective or holds promise, noting that, “we can begin to grow operational efficiencies around what has been or holds promise to become successful in regulatory settings.”

Meanwhile, in the United States, with high drug prices, shifting healthcare policies, and uncertainty surrounding the direction under the new Trump administration, Kimberly Westrich (Chief Strategy Officer, National Pharmaceutical Council) is advocating for a fundamental shift in healthcare policy to focus on what truly matters—ensuring patients receive the right treatment at an affordable cost.

“The current healthcare ecosystem in the United States sees drugs as an arbitrage opportunity to extract margin, rather than valuing drugs for how they help people get well, stay healthy, and avoid more costly care settings.”

Real-world data and evidence expansion
The evolving role of RWE highlights the need for a deeper understanding of how it can be optimized to address the specific priorities of healthcare decision-makers. For Rachele Hendricks-Sturrup the emphasis lies on the importance of addressing distinct evidentiary needs across regulators, payers, and HTA bodies. She advocates for a closer examination of these needs in 2025, particularly in identifying specific endpoints that, “align with what RWE can offer from both data and study design standpoints.”

This optimism is shared by Blythe Adamson (Head of Outcomes Research, Flatiron Health), who foresees a growing trend toward global standardization of RWE, driven by the harmonization of data models across countries. “Common data models will play a key role in enabling global evidence generation,” she explains. International collaborations, such as the Flatiron FORUM consortium, are expected to advance the understanding of evidence transportability across borders, enhancing the reliability and scalability of RWE.

Adamson also hopes for ongoing expansion of the RWD industry, with fit-for-purpose data types that cater to diverse use cases, enabling faster testing of new technologies and the scaling of research opportunities. Additionally, she anticipates the emergence of more adaptive designs in data quality. She told The Evidence Base:

“In 2025, I see more fluid types and qualities of RWD coming to market—more specifically, I expect there will be a more prominent element of adaptive design to ensure that the approach to data quality is reflective of its criticality to research, type of use case, and the complexity of curating it from source.”

For Sreeram Ramagopalan (Centre for Pharmaceutical Medicine Research, King's College London), the potential of synthetic data in generating RWE is key. However, he points to the need for rigorous demonstration projects to evaluate its validity. “Wider adoption of synthetic data will depend on showing validity compared to original RWD and ensuring transparency in synthetic data generation methods,” he suggests.

Nathan Buchbinder (Chief Strategy Officer, Proscia) predicts that 2025 will mark a breakthrough for pathology data. As he explained to The Evidence Base:

“We’ve seen this in the explosion of pathology-specific foundation models that emerged this year. Propelled by this momentum, I expect that life sciences organizations will increasingly augment their multimodal data with pathology real-world data to realize even more value.”

In his opinion, by prioritizing access to diverse, high-quality datasets and adopting centralized systems to enhance interoperability, organizations can develop robust AI models and drive breakthroughs such as biomarker discovery and faster development of companion diagnostics.

Buchbinder also highlights the growing collaboration between diagnostic laboratories and life sciences organizations.

“Diagnostic laboratories with digitized pathology data can increasingly help life sciences organizations to target patient recruitment in clinical trials. In this respect, it seems that the loop between research and clinical practice will increasingly close.”

Expanding on the potential of RWD, Jonathan Pearson-Stuttard (Head of LCP Health Analytics) places importance on the role of RWD in improving healthy equity. He explained to The Evidence Base that, “greater granularity in real-world data continues to provide novel insights into disparities in unmet disease need across equity sub-groups including according to income, ethnicity and other factors such as rural/urban location.” He anticipates that the FDA’s guidance on Diversity Action Plans for clinical studies will spur interest in developing RWE for equity-relevant sub-groups, aligning with payer priorities and addressing health disparities more effectively.

Terry Myerson (CEO, Truveta) envisions RWE insights fostering more dynamic and responsive scientific research. “We can expect new study designs that leverage real-time data, offering continuous monitoring of treatments even post-market,” he said. However, he stresses the importance of maintaining accountability, noting, “With great data comes great responsibility; maintaining data quality, transparency, and accountability remains crucial as regulatory standards evolve.”

As 2025 approaches, Myerson calls for stakeholders to embrace the exciting changes ahead.

“It's an exciting time that’s set to reshape how we think about evidence and innovation in medicine. Let's embrace this change with confidence and curiosity, knowing we are on the brink of something truly groundbreaking.”

Defining the role of AI in evidence generation
Tim Disher (Vice President, HEOR, Loon) predicts that 2025 will be a 'tipping point' for AI and machine learning (ML) tools, as their application expands from validation to active use in joint clinical assessments (JCAs) under the EU HTAR framework. “The last year has seen significant developments in AI applications to RCT screening, PICO scoping, and data extraction,” he notes. “The pressure to deliver timely, high-quality evidence for EU HTA submissions will force discussions about where AI can demonstrably outperform human capabilities.”

Disher also envisions an evolving HEOR landscape driven by AI advancements, shifting the field towards a strategic focus on AI oversight, methodology development, and appraisal of AI outputs. He highlights AI’s potential for 'superhuman' performance, sparking discussions on ethics, training, and the skillsets HEOR professionals need to succeed.

“In 2025, discussions will shift from questioning AI’s capability to actively exploring how to best integrate these powerful tools to maximize both efficiency and quality in evidence-based healthcare decision-making.”

Ben Bray (Evidence Generation Lead, LCP Health Analytics) also identifies productivity gains as the primary benefit of AI adoption in 2025. “The main prize here is productivity gains through automation... [and] to provide a speed boost to current workflows or enable whole new capabilities in the RWE and HEOR space,” he states. Like Disher, Bray hopes that next year will see the scaling up of AI adoption in specific use cases.

“I hope that 2025 will be the year that AI moves from promise to scaling up of adoption in specific use cases, particularly for approaches that move beyond generic chatbots to tools which meet the specific requirements of industry and stakeholders in RWE, HTA and HEOR.”

Sreeram Ramagopalan predicts that 2025 will see a broader adoption of AI across the RWE generation pipeline. While AI is already being used to analyze unstructured RWD, Ramagopalan anticipates further advancements in automating traditionally manual processes, such as protocol development and data analysis, to streamline and enhance efficiency in evidence generation.

Blythe Adamson agrees there will be a transformative shift in AI's role in evidence generation by 2025. “We’ll move from discussing potential applications of AI to real-world uses in evidence generation,” she predicts. A critical differentiator will be robust validation techniques to ensure AI is fit-for-purpose, whether through human oversight, ML, or a hybrid approach. “The key will be access to data at its source and high-quality labels,” she emphasizes.

Further predictions from Adamson see her highlight innovations in AI/ML and large language models (LLMs) as a means to responsibly and scalably learn from patient experiences. She predicts AI will unlock unprecedented speed and scale in RWD generation, transforming tasks that once required significant manual effort into efficient, repeatable processes.

“The potential use of ML in creating fit-for-purpose data is just beginning, I look forward to seeing how longitudinal datasets at scale can unlock additional innovative research in 2025.”

Rick Chapman (Chief Science Officer, Center for Innovation & Value Research) cautions against the potential pitfalls of AI, advocating for patient-centered and transparent applications. He warns of creating “a black box within a black box” when using AI to build cost-effectiveness models, which are already challenging for stakeholders to understand. “AI should address specific parts of a problem rather than attempt to build entire models,” Chapman explains. For instance, individual components designed with AI could be integrated into a validated model, enhancing trust and transparency.

Patient-centricity and health equity
Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and patient preferences are set to take center stage, according to Laura Dormer, Editor of The Evidence Base. She highlights a landmark development for the Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research in 2025: the mandatory inclusion of plain language summaries in all original research articles published in the journal. This move, Dormer notes, aims to, “support the accessibility of research findings to all those who will benefit from them, from patients to policymakers.”

Dormer also stresses the increasing importance of ensuring diverse patient representation in RWD, particularly as AI becomes more integral to its analysis. “With the expected growth in the use of AI to interrogate real-world data, it will be vital to ensure this data is representative of a diverse patient population,” she explains. “It is expected that HTAs will place more weight on PROs, and it would be great to see an increase in patient preference studies to examine more closely what patients themselves value in their own health management.”

This sentiment was echoed by Terry Myerson, who emphasizes the transformative role of RWD in addressing the limitations of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), particularly in capturing diverse patient experiences.

“Enter RWD, which promises more inclusive and representative data, capturing the complexity of real-world patient experiences. This shift could speed up the development and approval of therapies, making the process more efficient and insightful.”

For Jonathan Pearson-Stuttard, 2025 holds significant potential for innovative methodologies to address health inequalities, with a particular focus on the expanding use of distributional cost-effectiveness analysis (DCEA). “We expect market knowledge about the most appropriate use cases of DCEAs to be advanced materially in 2025,” he notes, emphasizing the methodology’s expanding role in evaluating interventions that foster equitable healthcare distribution. He points to a recent NICE submission as an exemplary use case, where DCEA was employed to quantitatively incorporate health equity considerations. This approach enabled allowances for evidence uncertainty and greater flexibility in the willingness-to-pay threshold.

Building on this focus, Tara Cowling (President, Medlior Health Outcomes Research) highlights value-based pricing (VBP) as another transformative approach to addressing health inequities. “VBP is an opportunity to measure and address health inequities, drive innovation, and ensure value and affordability for sustainable health systems”, she explains. By tying pricing to patient-centered outcomes and therapy response levels, VBP complements methodologies like DCEA by encouraging equitable access to treatments. Cowling stresses that incorporating broader measures of value, such as quality of life, employment, and caregiver impacts, can reduce disparities in health outcomes and foster a more inclusive healthcare system, further narrowing gaps in health equity.

Shifts in value-based healthcare towards broader value
Kimberly Westrich, author of the ‘Value Viewpoint’ series published on The Evidence Base, expresses optimism about a growing focus on broader value in healthcare in 2025: "Hope springs eternal: I believe we will see an increasing focus on value by many stakeholders in 2025."

She highlights key areas for change, including the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program under the Inflation Reduction Act.

“There will be continuing conversations about whether the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) are thinking about value as they implement the Inflation Reduction Act’s Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program… What evidence they say they considered may impact the incentives for generating real-world evidence on value in the future, in addition to the unintended consequences of the program for patients."

She also anticipates that employers, increasingly frustrated with traditional models and “fed up with the status quo”, will turn to value-based pharmacy benefits, which data indicates deliver savings three-times greater than rebate-based agreements.

Tara Cowling ascertains that VBP models will bring innovative, life-saving therapies to patients faster. To achieve this, she notes: “The critical component is negotiating pricing and payment based on the level of response to therapy (complete, partial, null) using measures of value determined through structured collaboration from the 5Ps: patients, providers, payers.”

Catrin Treharne (Health Economics Lead at LCP Health Analytics) highlights the growing challenges faced by many global governments related to sickness-related economic inactivity, particularly in the UK, where long-term sickness has driven unemployment to record levels. She emphasizes the well-established link between access to healthcare innovations and improved health outcomes, which play a critical role in keeping people economically active or supporting their return to work. However, Treharne notes, “The way we value and articulate the impact of healthcare interventions often fails to capture their broader contribution to societies and economies.”

Both Westrich and Treharne refer to advanced alternative methods as key for 2025 to better capture the full spectrum of healthcare value. They recognize the significance of the recent publication by Jason Shafrin, which introduces generalized cost-effectiveness analysis (GCEA) as a way to more comprehensively evaluating the societal value of health technologies. Treharne explains:

“With this combination of increased recognition as well as a growing body of proposed methods, the scene is set for tractable progress on more holistic value assessments by both HTA bodies and governments in 2025.”

In her recent Editorial discussing GCEA, Meng Li emphasizes the importance of ongoing development:

"The GCEA framework and methodology will continue to evolve through rigorous research and broader application. Both producers and consumers of value assessment research should take a more proactive role in developing methods and data to operationalize and enhance GCEA. This will ensure that our value estimates more effectively inform the decision-making needs of various stakeholders."

Weighing in on reimbursement policies for obesity treatments
Since their introduction, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have revolutionized obesity treatment, earning the title “Breakthrough of the Year 2023” from Science. Growing awareness of the health and economic burden of obesity-related comorbidities is pressing policymakers to identify viable solutions; however, implementing effective reimbursement policies remains a complex challenge.

Sreeram Ramagopalan notes the continued dominance of obesity treatments in 2025 discussions, particularly around reimbursement hurdles. “We are yet to see truly well-conducted studies on the real-world outcomes of GLP-1 receptor agonists, and hopefully 2025 will bring these, demonstrating the broad value and benefits these treatments deliver,” he states.

Jasim Uddin (Market Access Lead, LCP Health Analytics) points to a paradigm shift in how health systems approach obesity. “Health systems are moving away from viewing obesity as a lifestyle issue and increasingly recognizing it as a chronic disease that has reached ‘epidemic’ proportions—or at least as a major comorbidity contributing to numerous diseases,” he notes.

Uddin also highlights the rapid evolution in obesity treatments, with at least 16 products either approved or in Phase 3 development, including GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and tirzepatide. “For example, NICE in England currently has up to six technology appraisals in development or awaiting review in this space, many of which are likely to conclude in 2025,” he explains. Together, he stresses, these developments signal a transformative shift in reimbursement policies and practice.

“We will begin to see a paradigm shift that will drive policy change, which in turn will continue to drive innovation in this fast-evolving area. This will no doubt create challenges across RWE generation, HEOR and equitable patient access.”

The Evidence Base opinion
As RWE continues to gain prominence, it is increasingly recognized as a transformative opportunity across healthcare, highlighted by ISPOR naming it a top trend for 2024–2025. With emerging technologies generating more RWD than ever before, newer insights are driving advancements in patient care. Coupled with regulatory and HTA bodies signaling greater acceptance of RWE in decision-making, clearer expectations are emerging. This progress is likely to encourage companies to develop robust evidence generation plans that fully leverage RWD. By 2025, we anticipate seeing more companies integrate RWE into submission packages to support their therapies effectively, shaping a future where data-driven insights transform healthcare outcomes.

GLP-1 Receptor Agonists
GLP-1 receptor agonists, also known as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, GLP-1 analogs, or incretin mimetics, are a class of medications that have gained significant attention for their role in managing type 2 diabetes and, more recently, obesity. Here’s a comprehensive overview:

Mechanism of Action
GLP-1 receptor agonists mimic the actions of the body's natural GLP-1 hormone, which is released in response to food intake. They work by:

Increasing Insulin Secretion: When blood sugar levels are high, these drugs stimulate the pancreas to release insulin.
Suppressing Glucagon: They inhibit the release of glucagon from the pancreas, which helps reduce hepatic glucose production.
Slowing Gastric Emptying: By delaying how quickly food leaves the stomach, they help control the rise in blood sugar after meals.
Appetite Suppression: GLP-1 agonists signal to the brain to reduce appetite, leading to lower food intake and weight loss.

Key Benefits
Blood Sugar Control:
Effective in lowering HbA1c levels, providing substantial glucose control in type 2 diabetes patients.
Weight Management:
Proven to aid in weight loss, making them beneficial for diabetic patients who are also obese or overweight. Some are even approved specifically for weight loss in non-diabetic individuals with obesity.
Cardiovascular Benefits:
Several GLP-1 agonists have shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular death, particularly in patients with established cardiovascular disease.
Renal Protection:
There's evidence suggesting these drugs can slow the progression of chronic kidney disease in diabetic patients, reducing albuminuria and potentially delaying kidney failure.
Low Hypoglycemia Risk:
Unlike some other diabetes treatments, GLP-1 agonists have a lower risk of causing hypoglycemia because their insulinotropic effects are glucose-dependent.
Other Potential Uses:
Research is exploring their application in conditions like non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, Alzheimer's disease, addiction, and even certain cancers, as hinted at by posts on X.

Major Types and Administration
Short-Acting: Taken once or twice daily (e.g., exenatide twice daily).
Long-Acting: Administered weekly (e.g., semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide for once-weekly use). 
Oral Form: Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus) introduces the convenience of daily oral administration.

Most are administered via subcutaneous injection, although oral formulations are becoming available.

Side Effects and Considerations
Gastrointestinal Issues: Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation, which often subside over time.
Pancreatitis and Gallbladder Disease: There's an increased risk, though relatively rare.
Thyroid C-Cell Tumors: Animal studies have shown this risk, leading to caution in patients with a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Cost and Compliance: These medications can be expensive, and the need for injections might affect compliance.

Conclusion
GLP-1 receptor agonists have revolutionized the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity by offering benefits that extend beyond mere glucose control. They not only aid in weight management and cardiovascular health but also explore new frontiers in medical treatment. However, they come with considerations regarding side effects, costs, and administration methods. As with any medication, they should be prescribed based on an individual's health profile, managed by healthcare professionals, and monitored for efficacy and side effects.

For the first time in a decade, U.S. #obesity rates have declined slightly—from 46% in 2022 to 45.6% in 2023. While this is a step in the right direction, it has significant caveats. Morbid obesity rates continue to climb, and much of this modest progress is attributed to the increasing use of weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy.

As a physician, I can attest to the challenges of medication adherence. Even when medications work, consistently taking them is one of our greatest hurdles. These drugs often require lifelong use to maintain #weightloss. How do we convince #patients to stay on these treatments indefinitely, especially when side effects or costs become barriers?

These concerns highlight a bigger issue: overreliance on medications as a quick fix. While GLP-1 receptor agonists have proven effective, they don’t address obesity's root causes. Here are some broader concerns to consider:

Root Causes Remain Untouched: While medications may help people lose weight, they don’t fix unhealthy #diets, sedentary lifestyles, or environmental #toxins. Progress will always be limited without addressing these critical variables.

Sustainability and Access: With monthly costs often exceeding $1,000, how do we ensure equitable access? Many of those most affected by obesity cannot afford these treatments.

Long-Term Risks and Efficacy: Weight regain after stopping these medications is common, and side effects can further discourage adherence.

Moreover, while weight-loss medications are credited with this slight decline, other factors likely contributed. Post-pandemic lifestyle shifts and heightened awareness of obesity-related health risks—particularly in the South, where #COVIDー19 mortality was higher among people with obesity—may have played a role.

Medications are a valuable tool, but they are not a cure-all. For true and lasting progress, we need a holistic approach that goes beyond the prescription plan and integrates prevention, education, systemic changes, and long-term support.

The effectiveness of high taxes on sugar versus GLP-1 medications in reducing obesity involves different approaches, and the outcomes can depend on various factors such as policy enforcement, public health awareness, and accessibility of treatments. Here’s how the two compare:

High Taxes on Sugar

High taxes on sugary foods and beverages, like those implemented in some countries, aim to reduce consumption by making unhealthy options more expensive. The idea is to incentivize healthier choices and decrease the intake of excess calories from sugary drinks and foods, which are major contributors to obesity.

Evidence on Impact
•Studies on sugar taxes have shown mixed results. In some countries (e.g., Mexico, the UK), sugary drink consumption has decreased, and some evidence suggests small reductions in obesity rates, especially in low-income populations who might be more price-sensitive.
•However, reducing sugar consumption alone doesn’t always lead to significant reductions in obesity, as people may substitute sugary products with other high-calorie, low-nutrient foods or beverages.

Limitations
•Behavioral changes can take time and may not always be strong enough to combat deeply ingrained dietary habits.
•Some studies suggest that sugar taxes have more impact on consumption patterns but less direct influence on overall weight loss without a broader shift in lifestyle and diet.

GLP-1 Medications for Obesity

GLP-1 medications (like semaglutide and liraglutide) are designed to lower appetite, improve insulin sensitivity, and promote weight loss by mimicking a hormone (GLP-1) that regulates hunger and metabolism. These medications have been shown to be very effective for people with obesity or overweight by helping them lose significant amounts of weight (10–15% body weight on average).

Evidence on Impact
•Clinical studies have shown that GLP-1 medications can lead to substantial weight loss when combined with lifestyle changes. The weight loss tends to be sustained and has shown promise in reducing obesity-related health issues, such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and high blood pressure.
•Unlike sugar taxes, GLP-1 medications directly address the biological drivers of obesity, like hunger and satiety, which can result in more noticeable and quicker outcomes for weight loss.

Limitations
•Cost and accessibility: GLP-1 medications can be expensive and may not be widely accessible without insurance coverage. This limits their ability to reduce obesity across all population segments.
•Side effects: Some people may experience gastrointestinal issues (e.g., nausea) that can limit their use or effectiveness.

Comparison
•High taxes on sugar aim to create a long-term cultural shift by influencing consumer behavior at a population level. This strategy can help reduce sugar intake across a society but often requires additional public health measures, such as education, to be fully effective.
•GLP-1 medications can produce quicker and more individualized results, especially for those who are already struggling with obesity. These medications directly target the underlying mechanisms of hunger and metabolism, offering a potential solution for those who may not have been able to lose weight through diet and exercise alone.

Which Is More Effective?
•GLP-1 medications likely have a greater direct effect on weight loss for individuals with obesity, especially when combined with lifestyle changes, because they address the biological components of hunger and satiety.
•Sugar taxes can reduce sugar consumption at a population level, potentially leading to long-term benefits in reducing obesity rates, but they are less likely to produce the same degree of weight loss as GLP-1 medications.

Overall Impact

A combined approach—using taxes on sugary products to reduce overall consumption and GLP-1 medications to provide medical support for weight loss might be the most effective strategy for reducing obesity

Increases insulin release: Helps the pancreas produce insulin when blood sugar is high.

Reduces glucagon production: Lowers the amount of sugar produced by the liver.

Slows gastric emptying: Helps people feel fuller for longer, potentially aiding in weight management.

Uses:

Type 2 Diabetes Management: To lower blood sugar when combined with diet and exercise.

Ozempic is usually administered as a once-weekly injection under the skin (subcutaneously) in the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm.

Possible Side Effects:

Common: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, and reduced appetite.

Serious (rare): Risk of thyroid tumors, pancreatitis, kidney issues, or severe allergic reactions.

Important Notes:

Not recommended for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

It’s important to consult a healthcare provider before starting Ozempic to evaluate risks and benefits based on individual health needs.

Yes, individual variations in the metabolism of endogenous GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) can contribute to obesity. GLP-1 is a hormone secreted by the gut in response to food intake, and it plays a critical role in regulating appetite, glucose metabolism, and energy balance. Several factors can influence how quickly someone metabolizes GLP-1, which may affect weight regulation:
1.Variations in Enzyme Activity:
•The enzyme dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) rapidly degrades GLP-1 in the bloodstream. Some people may have higher activity levels of DPP-4, leading to faster breakdown of GLP-1 and reduced hormone activity. This can result in less effective appetite suppression and glucose regulation, contributing to obesity.
2.Genetic Differences:
•Genetic variations in the genes regulating GLP-1 production, secretion, or degradation can influence hormone levels and function. For example, polymorphisms in the GCG gene (which encodes the GLP-1 precursor) or the DPP4 gene may lead to differences in GLP-1 metabolism.
3.Gut Microbiome:
•The composition of the gut microbiota can affect GLP-1 secretion and its metabolic effects. Individuals with less favorable microbiomes may secrete less GLP-1 or experience altered degradation rates, potentially impacting weight regulation.
4.Obesity and Insulin Resistance:
•Paradoxically, obesity itself can impair GLP-1 secretion and signaling, creating a cycle where reduced GLP-1 activity exacerbates overeating and weight gain.
5.Inflammation and Chronic Conditions:
•Chronic inflammation, often associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome, can influence GLP-1 metabolism and signaling pathways.
6.Age and Lifestyle Factors:
•Factors like age, diet, and physical activity levels can affect GLP-1 secretion and degradation. For example, diets high in processed foods may impair gut hormone responses.

Implications for Treatment

These differences highlight why some individuals may benefit more from GLP-1-based therapies (like Ozempic or Wegovy) than others. These medications work by mimicking or enhancing GLP-1 activity, bypassing issues like rapid endogenous metabolism.

If you’re curious about your own GLP-1 metabolism, factors like genetic testing, glucose tolerance tests, or consultations with a metabolic specialist could provide insight.

Detailed Summary:

The review explores the effects of Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) on body composition, with a focus on lean body mass (LBM) and skeletal muscle in humans. These therapies are novel, glucose-lowering pharmacological interventions recommended as second-line treatments for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) when weight reduction is necessary. Both therapies have demonstrated clinically significant weight loss effects, though a substantial proportion of this weight loss includes reductions in lean body mass, not just fat mass (FM).

Key Findings:

General Observations:

1. Weight Reduction:

Both GLP-1RAs and SGLT2is induce weight loss primarily through fat mass reduction.

Lean body mass reductions, including skeletal muscle, constitute 20% to 50% of total weight lost across various studies.

2. Health Implications:

Loss of skeletal muscle mass may impair glycemic control and resting metabolic rate, increasing the risk of weight regain.

Decreased skeletal muscle strength and endurance can lead to frailty, higher risk of falls, and hospitalization.

Frailty risk is up to five times higher in T2DM patients compared to non-diabetic individuals.

What is GLP-1?

Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is a hormone secreted by the enteroendocrine L cells located in the small intestine and colon in response to food intake. It is an incretin hormone, meaning it stimulates insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner. GLP-1 plays a critical role in maintaining glucose homeostasis and regulating appetite.

---

Role of GLP-1 in the Body

1. Regulates Blood Sugar:

Stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells in response to elevated blood glucose levels.

Inhibits glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells, reducing hepatic glucose production.

2. Slows Gastric Emptying:

Reduces the speed at which food exits the stomach, leading to better glucose absorption and control over postprandial (after-meal) blood sugar levels.

3. Reduces Appetite:

Acts on the brain's hypothalamus to suppress hunger, promoting satiety and aiding in weight management.

4. Enhances Beta-Cell Function:

Stimulates the growth and survival of pancreatic beta cells, which produce insulin.

5. Improves Cardiovascular Health:

Lowers blood pressure and improves lipid profiles by reducing triglycerides and increasing HDL cholesterol.

How GLP-1 Affects Health

Positive Effects

1. Type 2 Diabetes Management:

GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide) are widely used as drugs to lower blood sugar levels in people with type 2 diabetes.

5. Gut Health:

Improves the gut microbiota by increasing beneficial bacteria through its role in nutrient signaling.

Health Issues Linked to Low GLP-1 Levels

1. Obesity:

Reduced GLP-1 secretion can lead to overeating and weight gain due to impaired appetite regulation.

2. Type 2 Diabetes:

Diminished GLP-1 response leads to poor glucose control and insulin resistance.

3. Metabolic Syndrome:

Low GLP-1 levels are associated with high blood pressure, dyslipidemia, and abdominal obesity.

How to Enhance GLP-1 Levels Naturally

Include GLP-1-stimulating foods such as high-protein meals, fiber-rich foods, healthy fats, and flavonoid-rich fruits and vegetables.

Regular exercise has been shown to improve GLP-1 secretion and enhance insulin sensitivity.

3. Probiotics and Prebiotics:

Foods that improve gut microbiota can increase GLP-1 secretion through the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs).

4. Avoid Overeating and Sugar Overload:

Excessive calorie intake and high-sugar diets can blunt GLP-1 secretion over time.

GLP-1 is a vital hormone for metabolic health, regulating blood sugar, appetite, and weight. Enhancing GLP-1 levels through diet, exercise, and in some cases, medication, can significantly improve outcomes for people with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related conditions. Research Objective:
This review explores the potential of food factors to improve glucose tolerance through the stimulation of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) secretion, emphasizing dietary peptides and flavonoids. GLP-1, a hormone released in response to food intake, plays a crucial role in insulin secretion, appetite suppression, and glucose metabolism.

Key Discoveries:

Role of Macronutrients:

Glucose and long-chain fatty acids are major stimulators of GLP-1 secretion through mechanisms involving nutrient transporters and G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).

Dietary proteins and peptides are potent GLP-1 secretagogues, with specific protein hydrolysates and amino acids showing significant effects in human and animal studies.

Unsaturated fatty acids stimulate GLP-1 secretion more effectively than saturated fats.

Effects of Dietary Peptides:

Peptides derived from protein digestion enhance GLP-1 secretion and inhibit dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4), an enzyme that degrades GLP-1.

Specific peptides, such as those derived from egg white protein and casein, exhibit high GLP-1 releasing activity.

Role of Flavonoids:

Phytochemicals, especially flavonoids like curcumin, quercetin, and genistein, stimulate GLP-1 secretion and improve glucose tolerance.

Flavonoids also exhibit antioxidative properties, enhance insulin sensitivity, and inhibit DPP-4, extending the half-life of GLP-1.

Resistant maltodextrin (RMD) and D-allulose are promising GLP-1 inducers. These factors improve glucose metabolism in animal models by directly or indirectly stimulating GLP-1-producing cells in the gut.

Mechanisms of Action:

GLP-1 secretion is triggered through nutrient sensing by enteroendocrine L cells in the gut. This involves:

Transport Proteins: Sodium-dependent glucose transporter-1 (SGLT-1) for glucose uptake.

Receptors: GPCRs like FFAR1 (GPR40), FFAR4 (GPR120), and the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) detect fatty acids, peptides, and amino acids.

Intracellular Signals: Increased intracellular calcium and cyclic AMP (cAMP) promote GLP-1 release.

Animal and Human Evidence:

High-protein meals significantly increase GLP-1 levels in both humans and animals, reducing postprandial blood glucose spikes and enhancing satiety.

Chronic administration of food factors like flavonoids and protein hydrolysates showed improved glucose tolerance in animal models.

Include protein-rich meals and flavonoid-rich foods (e.g., berries, onions, and green tea) to naturally stimulate GLP-1 secretion.

Formulate supplements and functional foods enriched with GLP-1-releasing peptides and flavonoids for individuals at risk of obesity and type-2 diabetes.

3. Future Research Directions:

Conduct human clinical trials to confirm the efficacy of GLP-1-releasing food factors and determine optimal dosages for therapeutic benefits.

Explore the molecular mechanisms of GLP-1 secretion in humans, focusing on the interactions between dietary components and enteroendocrine cells.

---

Conclusions

Food factors, particularly dietary peptides and flavonoids, show significant potential as safe and effective strategies to enhance GLP-1 secretion and improve glucose metabolism.

By combining nutraceutical approaches with pharmaceutical therapies, a synergistic effect could be achieved for managing metabolic diseases like obesity and diabetes.

The findings underscore the importance of dietary interventions as a preventive strategy for glucose intolerance and related disorders.

Yes, there are tests available to measure GLP-1 levels, although they are primarily used in research settings and not commonly performed in routine clinical practice. Here’s an overview:

---

Tests to Measure GLP-1 Levels

1. Blood Test for GLP-1

How it works: Blood samples are collected to measure GLP-1 concentrations using advanced biochemical techniques.

Methods:

ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay): A sensitive method to detect active or total GLP-1 levels.

RIA (Radioimmunoassay): An older but reliable method using radio-labeled antibodies to quantify GLP-1.

LC-MS/MS (Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry): A highly accurate method often used in research for detailed analysis.

Sample Requirements: Blood is typically drawn after fasting or postprandially (after a meal) to assess GLP-1 response.

Target Parameters:

Active GLP-1: The biologically active form, which stimulates insulin release.

Total GLP-1: Includes both active and inactive forms, providing an overview of secretion.

2. Postprandial GLP-1 Response Test

Description: Measures GLP-1 levels before and after consuming a standardized meal or glucose drink.

Purpose: Assesses the ability of the gut to secrete GLP-1 in response to food intake.

3. DPP-4 Activity Test

Description: Measures dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) enzyme activity, which degrades GLP-1. High DPP-4 activity can indicate reduced active GLP-1 levels.

Relevance: Often used in conjunction with GLP-1 tests in diabetes research.

4. Gut Hormone Panels

Description: Comprehensive panels measure multiple gut hormones (e.g., GLP-1, GIP, and PYY) to evaluate overall incretin function.

Purpose: Used in metabolic or obesity-related studies.

---

Challenges in Testing GLP-1

1. Short Half-Life: Active GLP-1 is rapidly degraded in the bloodstream (half-life ~1–2 minutes), requiring careful sample handling (e.g., DPP-4 inhibitors are added to blood samples to preserve GLP-1).

2. Specialized Labs: Testing for GLP-1 requires advanced equipment and expertise, so it’s usually performed in research or specialized diagnostic labs.

3. Variability: GLP-1 levels vary widely depending on factors like diet, time of day, and individual metabolic conditions.

---

Who Might Need GLP-1 Testing?

Research Participants: To study metabolic responses in obesity, diabetes, or gut health research.

Patients in Clinical Trials: Testing efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists or DPP-4 inhibitors.

Rare Clinical Cases: For individuals with unexplained hypoglycemia or gut hormone imbalances.

---

How to Access GLP-1 Testing

1. Research Centers: Often offered in metabolic or endocrinology research facilities.

2. Specialized Laboratories: Diagnostic labs equipped for advanced hormone testing.

3. Through Healthcare Providers: Rarely, endocrinologists may order these tests in collaboration with research facilities for specific medical needs.

---

While GLP-1 testing is not commonly required in clinical settings, advancements in understanding its role in metabolic health may lead to more widespread use in the future. For now, its application is mostly confined to research and drug development.

- **Class of Drugs**: They are a class of medications that mimic the effects of the incretin hormone GLP-1, which is naturally produced in the gut in response to food intake.

- **Mechanism of Action**:
  - **Insulin Stimulation**: They increase insulin secretion from the pancreas when blood glucose levels are high.
  - **Glucagon Suppression**: They decrease the release of glucagon, a hormone that increases blood sugar levels.
  - **Gastric Emptying**: They slow gastric emptying, which helps in controlling post-meal blood sugar spikes.
  - **Appetite Regulation**: They promote a feeling of fullness, leading to reduced calorie intake and weight loss.

### Medications in This Class:

- **Dulaglutide (Trulicity®)**
- **Exenatide (Byetta®, Bydureon®)**
- **Liraglutide (Victoza®, Saxenda®)**
- **Lixisenatide (Adlyxin®)**
- **Semaglutide (Ozempic® for diabetes, Wegovy® for obesity, Rybelsus® as oral form)**
- **Tirzepatide (Mounjaro®)**

### Clinical Applications:

- **Diabetes Management**: GLP-1 agonists are effective in lowering blood sugar levels in type 2 diabetes patients, often used when metformin alone isn't sufficient. They are recommended as first-line therapy for patients with cardiovascular risk or obesity.

- **Obesity**: Some GLP-1 agonists like liraglutide (Saxenda) and semaglutide (Wegovy) are approved for weight management in individuals with obesity or those who are overweight with at least one weight-related comorbidity.

### Benefits:

- **Blood Glucose Control**: Effective in reducing HbA1c levels.
- **Weight Loss**: Significant weight reduction due to appetite suppression.
- **Cardiovascular Protection**: Some GLP-1 agonists have been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.
- **Low Hypoglycemia Risk**: Unlike some other diabetes treatments, they pose a lower risk of hypoglycemia when used alone.
- **Other Health Benefits**: There is evidence suggesting benefits in managing or preventing conditions like non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, polycystic ovary syndrome, and even showing potential in areas like addiction treatment.

### Considerations:

- **Side Effects**: Common side effects include gastrointestinal issues like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. There have also been concerns about "Ozempic face" due to rapid weight loss affecting facial appearance.
- **Administration**: Most are injectable, taken either daily or weekly, with semaglutide also available in an oral form.
- **Cost**: These medications can be expensive, though manufacturer coupons and insurance might help offset costs.
- **Research**: Ongoing studies explore their use in other metabolic conditions and their long-term effects.

### Sentiment on X:

- There's a mix of excitement for their effectiveness in weight loss and diabetes management, alongside discussions on muscle loss risks, new research findings, and personal experiences of users feeling less drawn to unhealthy habits due to these drugs.

GLP-1 agonists represent a significant advancement in the pharmacological management of diabetes and obesity, offering benefits beyond simple glucose control, but they come with their own set of considerations regarding side effects, administration, and cost.

GLP-1 is produced in the intestine and binds to its receptor, GLP-1R, found in areas like the brain, heart, lungs, and kidneys.
Binding to GLP-1R sparks a series of responses: releasing insulin, reducing inflammation, and even protecting cells in the brain from stress.

GLP-1 improves gut health by supporting the mucosal lining, reducing inflammation in the digestive tract, and showing potential in treating inflammatory bowel diseases.

🧠 GLP-1 in Brain Health 🧠
It can cross the blood-brain barrier, making it a candidate for neurodegenerative diseases. In Parkinson’s, it prevents cell death and reduces toxic proteins. In Alzheimer’s, it shows promise in reducing neuroinflammation, boosting memory, and preventing cognitive decline.

🫁 Respiratory Benefits of GLP-1 🌬️
People with lung issues like asthma or even COVID-19 may benefit. GLP-1 can reduce inflammatory responses in the lungs, helping open airways and possibly even lowering hospital admissions for respiratory illnesses.

GLP-1 seems to support quicker wound healing and might improve conditions like psoriasis by decreasing inflammatory markers and boosting repair processes.

🛌 Type 2 Diabetes & Obesity 🛌
GLP-1’s main approved uses are still in blood sugar regulation and weight loss: It helps regulate insulin, reduce appetite, and improve metabolism, making it effective for Type 2 diabetes and even obesity treatment.

🔍 Studies on GLP-1 Analog Drugs 🔍
Liraglutide and Exenatide are GLP-1 analogs on the market, showing benefits across many of the issues above. They’re known for improving insulin sensitivity and reducing inflammation, opening new possibilities for treating diseases beyond diabetes.

Are there any bad side effects to the use of Ozempic
Answer
Ozempic (semaglutide) is primarily used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and, more recently, for weight management. While it's effective for many people, there are potential side effects and considerations:

Gastrointestinal Issues: The most common side effects include:
Nausea
Vomiting
Diarrhea
Constipation
Abdominal pain
Pancreatitis: There's an increased risk of pancreatitis, which can be serious. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain that may radiate to the back.
Hypoglycemia: Especially when used with other diabetes medications, Ozempic can lower blood sugar to dangerous levels, leading to dizziness, sweating, confusion, and if severe, loss of consciousness.
Kidney Injury: There have been reports of acute kidney injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing renal impairment.
Retinal Disorders: There's a potential risk for diabetic retinopathy complications, especially when blood sugar control improves rapidly.
Gallbladder Issues: Including gallstones, which might require surgery.
Allergic Reactions: Although rare, some people might experience allergic reactions ranging from mild to severe.
Cancers: There's been some concern about an increased risk of certain cancers, particularly thyroid C-cell tumors in animal studies. However, the direct risk to humans is still under investigation.
Injection Site Reactions: Pain, redness, or swelling where the injection is given.
Nutritional Deficiencies: Due to its impact on appetite and digestion, there might be concerns about deficiencies in vitamins or minerals over time.
Mental Health: Some people have reported mood changes, although this isn't as commonly documented as other side effects.

The concept of **eugenics**, historically, refers to efforts to improve human populations by controlling reproduction based on genetic traits. This is a highly controversial and unethical practice, associated with attempts to promote so-called "desirable" traits and eliminate "undesirable" ones.

There's been a lot of chatter on X recently claiming that the success of semaglutide-based weight-loss drugs falsifies all theories of obesity other than "you ate too much, you pig!".

I will refer to this as the CACO theory - calories in calories out. And I'll call the belief that CACO explains all obesity "CACO fundamentalism".

CACO fundamentalism is rather obviously false, and demonstrates the kinds of errors people make when they assume that any particular effect must have a single cause that is both sufficient and necessary. 

It is certainly the case that you can lose weight if you restrict your caloric intake enough. That's not in question. Semaglutide and other similar drugs help you do that, which is a good thing. 

It is probably also the case that some overweight comes from simple overeating - I say probably because it turns out to be remarkably difficult to make people obese by overfeeding them in a laboratory. But even if that's true it wouldn't follow that *all* overweight comes from overeating. In principle there could be many other causes. 

It has long been known that your body defends itself in conditions of scarce food by lowering your basal metabolic rate - so anything that does that is going to turn a constant intake of food into more fat on your body.

Anything else that lowers BMR will also tend to produce obesity even in people who eat modest portions of healthy food. It's not actually crazy to wonder if the general abandonment of smoking is one of the factors behind the rise in obesity since 1980; nicotine raises BMR, as do other stimulants.

CACO fundamentalism goes poof once we know that BMR is variable over a person's lifetime and can be changed by environmental factors; the end of widespread smoking is only the most obvious of the possibilities.

There are other more exotic theories  that something has gone wrong with the human mechanism for regulating the set-point of weight. It's possible that some kind of environmental contaminant  is messing that up.

I didn't write this post to advocate or dispute any of those theories, just to point out that any of them - or several of them - could still be true even though caloric restriction with semaglutide assistance works for weight loss.

Moralizing about the problem is unhelpful. Shame and guilt can only have a useful effect on the fraction of obese people who both (a) became obese solely through overeating, and (b) have enough self-discipline to rawdog calorie restriction without drugs like semaglutide. Metabolically Healthy Obese: Myth or Reality?

In the realm of health and wellness, few topics generate as much discussion and controversy as obesity. While the detrimental effects of excess weight are well-documented, a intriguing concept has emerged in recent years: metabolically healthy obesity (MHO). This phenomenon challenges our understanding of the relationship between body weight and health outcomes, prompting a closer examination of its implications for both individuals and healthcare professionals.

Defining Metabolically Healthy Obesity

Obesity is typically defined by a Body Mass Index (BMI) exceeding 30, or 25 for individuals of Pan-Asian descent. However, MHO refers to a subset of obese individuals who, despite their elevated BMI, exhibit none of the classic markers of metabolic syndrome. These individuals maintain normal blood pressure, lipid profiles, and glucose metabolism, seemingly defying the expected health consequences of excess weight.

The Spectrum of Metabolic Health

To better understand this phenomenon, researchers have delineated three distinct categories:

1. Metabolically Healthy Normal Weight (MHNW): Individuals with normal BMI and no metabolic abnormalities.
2. Metabolically Healthy Obese (MHO): Those with elevated BMI but no signs of metabolic syndrome.
3. Metabolically Unhealthy Obese (MUO): Obese individuals exhibiting clear evidence of metabolic dysfunction.

Studies suggest that 10-30% of obese individuals fall into the MHO category, a significant proportion that warrants closer examination.

The Implications of MHO

While the existence of MHO might seem reassuring, recent research paints a more complex picture. Longitudinal studies indicate that MHO may represent a transitional state rather than a stable condition. Within 6 to 15 years of diagnosis, many MHO individuals progress to the MUO category, developing the metabolic abnormalities they initially lacked.

This progression mirrors the development of other chronic conditions, such as the gradual onset of type 2 diabetes. The underlying mechanism appears to be related to increased inflammation associated with visceral (abdominal) fat accumulation.

Risk Assessment and Intervention

The concept of MHO underscores the importance of comprehensive health assessments beyond simple BMI calculations. While MHO individuals may not face immediate health risks, their long-term prognosis suggests an elevated risk for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and premature mortality.

This knowledge presents an opportunity for proactive intervention. Healthcare providers should work with MHO patients to implement lifestyle modifications and develop long-term health management strategies. In some cases, pharmacological interventions may be beneficial in transitioning from MHO to MHNW status.

It's worth noting that the risk of progression from MHO to MUO is not uniform across demographics. While younger MHO individuals may not face imminent health risks, older adults and postmenopausal women are at higher risk of transitioning to a metabolically unhealthy state.

The Power of Modest Weight Loss

Encouragingly, research indicates that even modest weight loss can yield significant health benefits. A reduction of just 5-10% of total body weight can substantially decrease the risk of long-term complications associated with obesity, including diabetes and heart disease.

Conclusion

The concept of metabolically healthy obesity challenges our binary understanding of weight and health. While it offers a more nuanced perspective on obesity, it should not be interpreted as a justification for complacency. Instead, it underscores the need for personalized health assessments and proactive interventions.

For professionals in fields intersecting with health and wellness, understanding MHO is crucial. It highlights the complexity of human metabolism and the importance of looking beyond simple metrics like BMI in assessing health risks.

By recognizing the transient nature of MHO and the potential for intervention, we can work towards more effective strategies for promoting long-term health and well-being. The journey to optimal health is multifaceted, and our approach to obesity management should reflect this complexity.

A drug approved to treat obesity in adults and teens is safe and effective for use in kids as young as 6 when combined with diet and exercise, a small new study shows.

Liraglutide lowered body mass, slowed weight gain and improved health markers in kids ages 6 through 11, according to research presented Tuesday at a medical conference and published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Based on the results of the trial, drugmaker Novo Nordisk has asked U.S. regulators to expand use of the medication for kids in that age group, a company spokesperson said Tuesday. If approved, the drug would be the first authorized to treat the most common type of obesity that affects more than 20% of U.S. kids ages 6 through 11, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

“To date, children have had virtually no options for treating obesity,” said Dr. Claudia Fox, a pediatric obesity expert at the University of Minnesota who led the study. “They have been told to ‘try harder’ with diet and exercise.”

Side effects were common among those given the drug, particularly gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. And experts said doctors and parents would need to carefully consider those risks and the lack of data about the long-term use of such drugs in young kids.

“Having a medication for that age group, if approved, would be a really nice tool to have, but we’re also going to have to be careful about how widely we start using it,” said Dr. Melissa Crocker, a pediatric obesity specialist at Boston Children’s Hospital who wasn’t involved in the study. “And I would answer that differently at 6 than I would at 11.”

Liraglutide is in a class of so-called GLP-1 drugs that include blockbuster medications like Wegovy and Mounjaro. The medications mimic hormones that affect appetite, feelings of fullness and digestion. It’s taken as a daily injection and is approved under the brand name Victoza to treat diabetes in adults and children ages 10 and older and as Saxenda to treat obesity in adults and children ages 12 to 17.

The new study, paid for by Novo Nordisk, included 82 children with a mean age of 10 and a baseline weight of about 155 pounds (70 kilograms). The average starting BMI was 31, above the threshold for childhood obesity. More than half the children had obesity-related health problems such as insulin resistance, asthma or early puberty. The results were presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Madrid.

In the trial, 56 children received daily injections of up to 3 milligrams of liraglutide for nearly 13 months, while 26 got dummy medications. The kids were followed for six months afterward.

All the children received individual counseling to help them follow a plan that called for a healthy diet and 60 minutes a day of moderate to high-intensity exercise.

Researchers found that kids who took the drug for more than a year reduced their body mass index -- a measure of height and weight that can account for a child’s natural growth – by 5.8%. Children who received the dummy medication saw their BMI increase by 1.6%.

At the same time, children who received the drug slowed weight gain to 1.6% of their body weight during that period, compared with a 10% gain for those who got sham drugs.

The study found that 46% of kids who got the drug lowered their BMI by at least 5%, an amount that has been linked to improvements in health problems tied to obesity. In kids who received placebo, 9% met that mark. Lower measures of blood pressure and blood sugar were detected in children who received the drug, researchers noted.

Side effects, mostly mild to moderate, were reported in nearly 90% of both groups of participants. Gastrointestinal side effects including nausea and vomiting were reported in 80% of kids who received the drug, compared with 54% who received sham medications. Serious side effects were reported in seven children using liraglutide and two who took placebo. Six participants taking the drug left the trial because of the side effects, while no one taking placebo stopped treatment.

In the six-month follow-up, children in both groups who stopped treatment increased BMI and gained weight, the study found. The trial has been extended to include more treatment and follow up, with results expected in 2027.

Fox receives research funding from Novo Nordisk and drugmaker Eli Lilly paid directly to her institution. Those companies are also conducting trials with more powerful weekly injections of Novo’s Wegovy and Lilly’s Zepbound in kids as young as 6.

Dr. Alaina Vidmar, a pediatric obesity specialist at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles who wasn’t involved in the new study, said she has used liraglutide off-label to treat young kids and would welcome approval of the drug to increase flexibility and access.

The drug treats the underlying physiology of obesity, which is a complex, chronic disease that can occur at any age. Early use can prevent obesity and life-threatening health problems from extending into the teen years — and adulthood.

“We want these kids to have long, healthy lives,” Vidmar said. “The sooner that we can start, the more likely we can stop them from getting early onset diabetes, early onset heart disease, sleep apnea, all of those things. Doing nothing is not the right answer.”

Whether we are starving or feel full is a state controlled by our brain, more precisely the hypothalamus. This small region in the center of our brain contains #neurons that release signals telling us whether we are hungry or satiated. Our goal is to establish a #humanbrainmodel of appetite regulation to provide a platform for metabolism and obesity research. 
 
#Obesity affects 1 in 8 people worldwide and is connected to devastating comorbidities like #cancer or #cardiovasculardiseases. A human model of these neural networks can shed light on appetite regulation and help develop and understand weight-lowering medication such as Wegovy. 
 
Our group has developed a protocol to generate key #hypothalamicneurons such as the hunger neurons AGRP and satiety-promoting POMC neurons. This stem cell-derived model allows us to both unravel their embryonic development in human and perform functional studies by treating the neurons with hormones and obesity drugs to record their functional response.

Ozempic (semaglutide) is a medication primarily used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and, more recently, for weight management. Here are some of the common and notable side effects associated with Ozempic:

- **Gastrointestinal Issues:** These are among the most common side effects and can include:
  - Nausea
  - Vomiting
  - Diarrhea
  - Constipation
  - Abdominal pain

- **Decreased Appetite:** Which can lead to weight loss, which might be intended in weight management but can be unexpected in diabetes treatment.

- **Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar):** Especially if used in combination with other diabetes medications like sulfonylureas or insulin. Symptoms might include dizziness, sweating, confusion, and shakiness.

- **Pancreatitis:** There's a risk of developing pancreatitis, which can be serious. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain that might radiate to the back, nausea, and vomiting.

- **Kidney Problems:** There have been reports of acute kidney injury, particularly in patients with existing kidney issues.

- **Gallbladder Issues:** Including gallstones, which might require surgical intervention in some cases.

- **Injection Site Reactions:** Such as pain, redness, or swelling at the site where Ozempic is injected.

- **Allergic Reactions:** Although rare, some individuals might experience allergic reactions which could be severe, including rash, itching, swelling, severe dizziness, or trouble breathing.

- **Thyroid Tumors:** In animal studies, semaglutide caused thyroid C-cell tumors. While the relevance to humans isn't entirely clear, it's a consideration, especially for those with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

- **Vision Changes:** Some users have reported changes in vision, which might be related to rapid changes in blood sugar levels.

- **Heart Rate Increase:** There might be an increase in heart rate, which could be concerning for individuals with heart conditions.

- **Mental Health:** There have been reports of depression or suicidal thoughts, though these are less common.

It's important for anyone considering or using Ozempic to discuss these potential side effects with their healthcare provider. The benefits versus risks should be evaluated based on individual health conditions and needs. Also, not everyone will experience these side effects, and many might find them manageable or temporary as the body adjusts to the medication. Always consult with a healthcare professional for advice tailored to your specific situation.

Weight loss treatment options can be broadly categorized into #lifestyle changes, medications, and surgical interventions. Here's an overview:

**1. *Lifestyle Changes:*
   - **Diet:** 
     - **Low-calorie diets:** Reducing overall calorie intake.
     - **Low-carb diets:** Like ketogenic or Atkins, which focus on reducing carbohydrate intake.
     - **Mediterranean diet:** Rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts and seeds, and olive oil, with moderate amounts of fish, poultry, dairy, and red wine.
     - **Intermittent Fasting:** Patterns like 16/8 (fast for 16 hours, eat in an 8-hour window) or 5:2 (eat normally for 5 days, restrict calories for 2 days).
   - **Exercise:** 
     - **Aerobic Exercise:** Activities like walking, running, cycling, or swimming.
     - **Strength Training:** Helps in building muscle mass which can increase metabolism.
     - **High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT):** Short bursts of intense exercise alternated with less-intense recovery periods.

   - **Behavioral Changes:**
     - **Mindful Eating:** Paying attention to hunger cues and eating without distraction.
     - **Sleep:** Adequate sleep can influence weight regulation hormones.
     - **Stress Management:** Techniques like yoga, meditation, or even hobbies can reduce stress-related eating.

**2. *Medications:*
   - **Prescription Medications:**
     - **Orlistat (Xenical, Alli):** Reduces fat absorption in the gut.
     - **Liraglutide (Saxenda):** An injectable that mimics the effects of GLP-1, which helps regulate blood sugar levels and appetite.
     - **Phentermine-Topiramate (Qsymia):** Combines a weight loss drug with a seizure medication to reduce appetite and increase feelings of fullness.
     - **Naltrexone-Bupropion (Contrave):** Combines an opioid antagonist with an antidepressant to reduce appetite and manage cravings.
     - **Semaglutide (Wegovy):** Similar to liraglutide, also works on GLP-1 receptors.

   - **Over-the-counter (OTC) Supplements:**
     - **Garcinia Cambogia:** Contains hydroxycitric acid which might block fat production.
     - **Green Coffee Bean Extract:** High in chlorogenic acids, which might help with weight loss.
     - **Raspberry Ketones:** Claimed to increase the breakdown of fat.

**3. *Surgical Interventions:**
   - **Bariatric Surgery:**
     - **Gastric Bypass:** Reduces the size of the stomach and bypasses part of the small intestine.
     - **Sleeve Gastrectomy:** Removes a large portion of the stomach, leaving a banana-shaped section.
     - **Adjustable Gastric Band:** A band is placed around the stomach to create a small pouch above the band.
     - **Biliopancreatic Diversion with Duodenal Switch:** A more complex surgery that removes a portion of the stomach and reroutes the small intestine.

**4. *Alternative Therapies:**
   - **Acupuncture:** Some people use acupuncture to help with appetite control.
   - **Hypnotherapy:** Aimed at changing eating behaviors through hypnosis.

**Important Considerations:**
- **Consultation:** Always consult with healthcare providers before starting any weight loss program, especially medications or surgery, due to potential side effects and health risks.
- **Sustainability:** Lifestyle changes are generally recommended as they can lead to sustainable weight loss. Quick fixes often result in weight regain.
- **Health Checks:** Regular monitoring of health parameters like blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol is crucial during weight loss.

Remember, the effectiveness of these treatments can vary greatly between individuals, and what works for one person might not work for another. Always tailor treatments to individual health needs and preferences.

"Exploring Modern Approaches to Weight Loss and Health"

In today's fast-paced world, achieving and maintaining a healthy weight has become more challenging than ever. Yet, with advancements in science and technology, there are more options available than ever before to help individuals lose weight and improve their overall health. Here's a breakdown of the most popular and effective strategies.

1. Balanced Diets

The foundation of any weight loss journey is a balanced diet. Instead of following fad diets that often lead to temporary results, many experts recommend focusing on whole foods, fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains. The Mediterranean diet, for example, emphasizes these foods along with healthy fats like olive oil. It's known for its heart health benefits and sustainability, making it a favorite among nutritionists.

2. Low-Carb and Ketogenic Diets

Low-carb diets have gained popularity for their effectiveness in rapid weight loss. The ketogenic (keto) diet, in particular, involves reducing carbohydrate intake to a minimal level and increasing fat consumption. This shift pushes the body into a state of ketosis, where it burns fat for energy instead of carbs. While effective, it's important to follow this diet under medical supervision, as it can have side effects.

3. Intermittent Fasting

Intermittent fasting (IF) has emerged as a popular trend, where individuals alternate between periods of eating and fasting. The 16/8 method, where one fasts for 16 hours and eats during an 8-hour window, is one of the most common approaches. IF not only aids in weight loss but also offers benefits like improved metabolic health and increased longevity.

4. Exercise and Physical Activity

No weight loss strategy is complete without exercise. Regular physical activity, whether it’s cardio, strength training, or flexibility exercises, is crucial for burning calories and building muscle. High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) has become particularly popular for its efficiency short bursts of intense exercise followed by rest can burn more calories in less time compared to traditional workouts.

5. Behavioral Therapy

Sometimes, the key to weight loss lies not just in what we eat or how we move, but in our mindset. Behavioral therapy helps individuals identify and change unhealthy eating habits, manage stress, and develop a positive relationship with food. Techniques such as mindful eating, where individuals pay attention to their hunger cues and eating experiences, can lead to more sustainable weight loss.

6. Medical Interventions

For those struggling with significant weight issues, medical interventions might be necessary. Prescription medications like orlistat, liraglutide, and semaglutide can assist with weight loss by reducing appetite or fat absorption. However, these should only be used under the guidance of a healthcare professional due to potential side effects.

7. Bariatric Surgery

In cases of severe obesity, bariatric surgery might be an option. Procedures like gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, and adjustable gastric banding can lead to substantial weight loss by altering the digestive system. While effective, these surgeries come with risks and require lifelong changes in diet and lifestyle.

8. Wearable Technology and Apps

Technology has made it easier than ever to track and manage health. Wearable devices like fitness trackers monitor physical activity, heart rate, and even sleep patterns, helping users stay on top of their fitness goals. Additionally, smartphone apps provide calorie counting, workout routines, and even meditation guides, making it easier to integrate healthy habits into daily life.

9. Alternative Therapies

Some people explore alternative therapies for weight loss, such as acupuncture, hypnosis, or herbal supplements. While the evidence supporting these methods varies, they may complement other weight loss strategies for those looking for a more holistic approach.

~ With so many options available today, losing weight and getting healthy is more accessible than ever. However, it’s important to remember that there is no one-size-fits-all solution. The best approach is one that aligns with your personal preferences, lifestyle, and health needs. Consulting with healthcare professionals and staying informed about the latest research can help you find the most effective strategy for your journey to better health.

A new study at St. Vincent's University Hospital (SVUH) suggests that weight-loss medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy, or Monjaro may not just suppress appetite but also speed up metabolism.

A randomised controlled trial led by Professor Donal O’Shea, SVUH and UCD School Of Medicine found a strong relationship between the amount of weight lost and increases in metabolic activity caused by daily use of medications based on the hormone Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1).

The findings published in the Journal of the Obesity Society challenge the belief that recent weight loss medications work just by simply causing those who use them to eat less.

“It always seemed oversimplistic to me that these new treatments were just making people eat less,” said Professor O’Shea.

“So, this study finding is an exciting step forward in our understanding of how these new medicines for obesity work.”

Adding: “This study challenges the main narrative about these newer treatments which is that they simply make you eat less, and that any action on energy burn is minimal.

“The findings also provide science to support the fact that the treatment of obesity is not simply to eat less and move more – that’s the prevention piece – treatment is more complex than that.”

In the randomised controlled trial, which involved 30 patients, those who had low metabolic activity before starting treatment benefited the most from medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Monjaro.

The patients had specialised imaging of the fat within their abdomen using a PET-CT scanner, with scans carried out before and after six months of treatment.

The results showed a strong correlation between increased metabolic activity and the degree of weight loss. Furthermore, those with low metabolic activity before starting treatment benefited the most from it.

“The strength of the association is surprising given the relatively small numbers studied and suggests this increase in metabolic activity is a significant contributor to how these drugs work,” said Professor O’Shea.

“Safe medical treatment for obesity is still in its infancy and we need to understand fully how the treatment works. Understanding how these agents increase energy burn should be an important part of future research.

“I hope the companies involved in the development of these treatments will examine this area in more detail because these are very expensive studies to carry out and we are very grateful to the Health Research Board and University College Dublin for supporting it.”

The study ‘GLP‐1 therapy increases visceral adipose tissue metabolic activity: lessons from a randomised controlled trial in obstructive sleep apnea’ was co-authored by Professor Silke Ryan, SVUH, funded by the @hrbireland and supported by University College Dublin.
